newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey to launch own eurobond trade in Istanbul.
newsitem.headline: Turkey to launch own eurobond trade in Istanbul.

text.p: Turkey will launch an international bond market next week to boost trade in Turkish Eurobonds and increase long-term debt availability, a senior Istanbul stock exchange official said on Friday.
"The market will open on February 18, or at worst, one week later," Huseyin Erkan, executive vice-chairman of the Istanbul Stock exchange, told Reuters.

The new bond market, which will be set up in a free trade zone under the auspices of the Istanbul stock exchange, would cut out the high costs and effort currently hindering trade in Turkish Eurobonds.

"What it will do is to provide high liquidity. When the liquidity is high the spreads will be lower, and when the spreads are lower, more international money is going to be attracted to these markets," he said.
Erkan said he expected trading to reach around $50 million a day by the end of the first year.
Erkan said the only trading ground for Turkish Eurobonds at present was a disorganised over-the-counter market in London, with daily trading only about two million dollars.
Some 60 percent of the bonds were owned by Turkish banks, he said, who had to trade through market makers in London with very wide spreads.
"When this organised market opens up the participants in London will also take advantage of this market, and we are allowing for arbitrage opportunities," Erkan said.
Settlement will be through the central depository Takasbank in Turkey.
Erkan said about $13 billion of Turkish Eurobond stock was outstanding at the moment, about 60 percent in Japanese yen and the rest in German marks and dollars.

In a bid to extend its maturities from the usual six-to-nine-month segments necessitated by the volatile Turkish lira and to reduce sky-high interest rates, Turkey has been investing in Eurobonds since the late 1980s.
But in 1994, when the country was reeling under an economic crisis, it was unable to launch any.

Turkey launched a seven-year 500-million mark Eurobond last week, and expects to raise some some $2 billion in international capital markets this year mainly in mark, dollar and yen. Turkey borrowed $2.9 billion last year.

Although domestic bond yields have come down by around 25 points since late last year to the high 80s, bankers say the Turkish currency needs to win a lot more confidence before the government can borrow for much more than a year in Turkish lira.

The lowering of Turkey's foreign debt rating by three credit rating agencies, including Standard and Poor's, in December was the latest factor to chill foreign interest. Moody's has warned it could follow suit and lower Turkey's Ba-3 rating.
"(This market) will ultimately allow the Turkish treasury to issue these Eurobonds a lot more easily in the future and with more favourable rates," Erkan said.

Turkey currently has about $75 billion of foreign debt. But only $13 billion of this is in Turkish Eurobonds -- the rest are direct bank loans, project credit, government loans and sovereign bonds, which are much more difficult to securitise.

"(Issuing Eurobonds) is really a matter of recscheduling the debt," Erkan said. "If the short-term debt is totally in Turkish liras and the budget deficit is actually equal to the servicing of the short-term debt, then we are talking about a short-term scheduling problem."
Currently Turkish banks refrain from trading in Eurobonds because of the high tax on profits -- which can be as high as 45 percent. The new market will be tax exempt.

The inaugration of the new bond market will coincide with the beginning of trading on the Istanbul exchange's international equity market, which opened in September to allow foreign institutions to list in Istanbul tax-free.
Erkan said no company had been listed on that market so far but he expected an unidentified U.S. bank to list about 15 of its funds very soon.
